idiom_name: status/count return plus errno, enforced with warn_unused_result or C23 [[nodiscard]]
implementation_notes: C brings no return-value convention of its own: the classic discipline is a hand-written pair of (returned status, errno), for example write() returning the number of bytes written and -1 on failure, with errno meaningful only when the return indicated an error. What replaces the structure is tooling plus discipline - glibc declares its important functions with the warn_unused_result attribute and C23 standardises [[nodiscard]] on functions and on struct/union/enum return types, so the compiler can warn when a caller drops a result. The classic 'return a status and pass the real value out through a pointer' form is still justified for multiple outputs and for ABI-stable APIs, but returning a small struct by value is usually the clearer way to give the caller something to act on.
pitfalls: A discarded result is invisible: C has no warning by default, and errno is only meaningful when the return value indicated an error - and only until the next library call overwrites it.

Casting to void does not reliably silence warn_unused_result in GCC (the cast can be stripped before the warning pass); binding the result to a variable, or a deliberate if (write(...)) {} , is the accepted escape hatch.
In-band sentinels collide with data: -1, 0 and NULL all double as valid results somewhere in the C library, so the caller must know which sentinel applies to which call.
